title: 'Son of man' title taken from the Parables of Enoch

tellings.quote: The proper title the son of man comes from first Enoch specifically from the second section of first Enoch which is called the parables.
And I asked the =angel= who went with me and showed me all the hidden things, concerning that Son of Man, who he was, and whence he was, (and) why he went with the Head of Days?

And he answered and said unto me: This is the Son of Man who hath righteousness, With whom dwelleth righteousness, And who revealeth all the treasures of that which is hidden, Because the Lord of Spirits hath chosen him, And whose lot hath the pre-eminence before the Lord of Spirits in uprightness for ever.
And at that hour that Son of Man was named In the presence of the Lord of Spirits, And his name before the Head of Days.
For from the beginning the Son of Man was hidden, And the Most High preserved him in the presence of His might, And revealed him to the elect.

And he sat on the throne of his glory, And the sum of judgement was given unto the Son of Man, And he caused the sinners to pass away and be destroyed from off the face of the earth, And those who have led the world astray.

plain: Jesus's title "the Son of Man" was taken from an older Jewish book, the researcher Tim Alberino tells Michels: from 1 Enoch, an ancient text left out of most Bibles, and "specifically from the second section," called the Parables. If so, the gospels would be drawing on a figure that Enoch's book had already described. In R. H. Charles's 1917 translation, Enoch asks his guiding angel about "that Son of Man, who he was, and whence he was," and is told "This is the Son of Man who hath righteousness" and "who revealeth all the treasures of that which is hidden." The book says "from the beginning the Son of Man was hidden," that he "was named in the presence of the Lord of Spirits," and that he sat "on the throne of his glory" and "the sum of judgement was given unto the Son of Man." So the Parables do use the title again and again for a hidden, chosen figure who judges the world; whether the gospel writers took it from there is the teller's reading, which the book by itself can neither show nor rule out.
